text: The king, a Kṣatriya well-versed in righteousness and bearing the responsibility of protecting his subjects, after punishing those deserving punishment, should uphold truth and Dharma everywhere. Having established the subjects who are devoted to the duties of their respective social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), the benevolent ruler should nourish them at the proper time for the satisfaction of the gods. The gods, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, ancestors (Pitṛs), sages, and whoever others are glorified through sacred rites such as sacrifices and oblations... The wise know that gratifying the gods through worship and sacrifices is Devayajna, while gratifying subjects and guests with food and hospitality is Nriyajna/Pitriyajna. The timely feeding and gratification of cows and other living beings is declared as Bhutayajna; and Rishiyajna and the others have been specified in order by the sages. Gratifying the sages is held to be achieved through sacred study, teaching, japa, and gifts. Therefore, among all sacrifices, Devayajna is considered the primary one. But Bhutayajna is second, and in my view it is the very basis of Devayajna. Therefore, in all lands, the king (ruler of the earth) must be committed to protection. The king should nurture both Devayajna and Bhutayajna alike. The wise declare that Devayajna yields its full fruit only when performed with pure offerings and materials. The primary material worthy of sacrifice is declared to be crops/grains (sasya) and the like. The Earth, whose fruit is the yield of crops, was sustained by Vishnu in his Varaha (boar) incarnation. Formerly, Lord Vishnu, desiring the welfare of the world, saved her from falling into/drinking the waters of the netherworld, and that Supreme Person who holds the Sharnga bow was implored by the Goddess Earth. With joy, he proclaimed the greatness of the Earth in the presence of the gods: "Because she holds gems and riches within her womb, she is called Ratnagarbha and Vasundhara." Because she streams forth grains, medicinal plants, and water, the Earth is known as Medini, enhancing the life-force of living creatures. All classes of living beings—two-footed, four-footed, and various egg-born creatures—exist through the magnificent essence of Medini. Having attained life and vigor, creatures surely subsist on earth—including serpents, as well as other two-footed and four-footed animals. By nourishing beings and bestowing life, eternal delight of the gods is secured, leading to the practice of truth and righteousness which yields the fruit of the four human goals (chaturvarga). Thus creation becomes fruitful and the Creator rejoices. Therefore, grain (sasya) is the very life-breath of the earth and the noble livelihood derived from her. The gods call grain (sasya) the auspicious wedding thread (mangalyasutra) of the Earth; indeed, crops are the vital pulse (jivanadi) embodying the living energy of Medini. Produce (sasyādi) is indeed the supreme virtue and highest glory of the earth. Full of crops, the earth (vasumatī) enhances the life-force of all living beings. She is the bestower of all auspiciousness, the granter of satisfaction to the gods, ever-bearing crops, and especially flowing with sweet water.

Abiding by the command of Viṣṇu, the earth shines everywhere. Protected by Viṣṇu, the land is the mother of the continuous stream of living beings. She is the nourisher, the primordial mother, bestowing nourishment and contentment; holding gems within her womb, she eternally affords complete protection to all. Having high mountains as her breasts, the ocean as her girdle, and richly adorned with ocean pearls, this goddess of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow (Viṣṇu) shines resplendent. With the sun, moon, and fire as her lamps, fanned by gentle breezes, and possessing vast forests for roaming, this earth is the beloved of Viṣṇu. All-enduring, she shines here, established across the circle of directions. The king should divide this entire earth, radiant with lands suitable for agriculture, into various regions of diverse forms. Surrounded by the ocean on all sides since creation, this land was indeed created level everywhere by Brahmā, the creator. Bestowing diverse fruits across various aeons (kalpas), she is praised by hosts of gods, gandharvas, sages, and kings. Yielding fruit full of vitality and cherished in every kalpa, this vast land sometimes sank into the floods of ocean waters. In some places, its interior regions are exposed by the ocean, and in some places, its channels are split open according to the changes of time over aeons. Flowing with rich and poor streams, taking low and elevated forms, the earth in certain places is divided by mountains and rivers. It possesses large rivers, fertile land, and expansive lakes; in some places it is gravelly, and in others extremely hot in nature. Gradually, this earth has become waterless in certain areas, saline or barren in others, and in some places destructive to seeds. Thus, this earth is declared to have become manifold in nature; therefore, a king consecrated to the protection of all living beings... ...should examine auspicious land for the growth of crops—land that is free from bones, stone fragments, and the like, and possesses soft soil. It should be well-moistened, slightly reddish or black in color, free from husk and glass, fertile, and radiant with moisture and sap. It should have no pits, be neither unfathomably deep nor excessively elevated, but level, and vibrant with the fragrance of mallikā, jātī, kuṭaja, and wine. Or it may bear the fragrance or exudation of lotus, date-palm, and tiniśa, possessing water that does not dry up, or water that constantly retains its drinkable quality. It should rapidly promote the growth of seeds, yield comfort to the furrow, be covered with bull-foam, and be endowed with gentle living creatures. It should be free of thorns and dried dung, dense and compact, heavy in weight when weighed, and conducive to the growth of medicinal plants. Land is classified as Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatra, Vaiśya, Śūdra, or in certain places as land with mixed attributes according to preference. Thus divided into five types by class, possessing clear water, internal fertility as well as external richness, and suitable for cultivation...

It should bring delight to the eyes, be free from anthills and harmful creatures, and be inhabited by gentle birds. Even if subject to violent winds, whirlwinds, or the fury of fire, its subterranean waters remain unconsumed, and it promotes the growth of inner gardens and orchards. Bestowing growth to shady trees, moderately sloped, and repeatedly promoting the growth of various rows of seeds. Soft to the touch, highly pleasing to cattle and livestock, endowed with auspicious characteristics, and having very few defects anywhere. Easily draining water and easily absorbing water, surrounded in places by threshing-floor land possessed of such characteristics. Seeing such excellent land, the king should acquire it here; prompted by the king, virtuous experts well-versed in the procedure of land-testing [should inspect it]. Whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, they should be knowledgeable in the principles of water-divining (dagārgala) and proficient in agricultural science. They should examine the land on an auspicious day under favorable omens, having bathed, being pure, wearing clean clothes, and wearing a gold finger-ring. Reaching the designated land, the wise expert should circumambulate it clockwise amidst auspicious sounds and recitations of benedictory verses (svasti-vākya). In the evening or in the morning, along with Vedic scholar Brāhmaṇas, it should be purified with pure pañcagavya or sacred water. Digging with a spade, a balance, or a chisel in places, the wise person should examine the soil after inspecting it again and again. Smelling, tasting, or weighing the soil in places, or putting it in water inside a pot for up to a ghāṭikā, the expert evaluates it. One should know the characteristics of the land through color, droplets, taste, and seepage; land that is uniform in color, uniform in shade, dense, and glossy is ideal. Declared by sages to be praised even for gods and kings, such land bestows safety and growth upon Brāhmaṇas and Vaiśyas as well. Earth possessing auspicious characteristics bestows good fortune upon all, constantly granting health to the family and increase of wealth, cattle, and grain. The scholar of soil characteristics should designate land as excellent, or as medium in places, and should diligently avoid inferior land. "This land is fit for agriculture, this one is favored for gardens, this land is prescribed for forests, and this one is designated for water reservoirs." This is declared as the fourth [type of] land by nature. Thus, at an auspicious time, land should be designated by order of the king. One who desires land must mark the boundaries and areas in villages, regions, forts, and cities as well. The wise one, who knows the nature of various fields and water sources, should skillfully designate land up to the palace borders suitable for agriculture, gardens, etc., for the happiness and success of living beings. With the help of eminent artisans who know measurements and are versed in scriptures, the king should undertake the construction of villages, forts, and cities.

In the midst of forests, on riverbanks, or on mountain slopes, particularly here and there within his own country and realms— —he should establish cowherd settlements (*ābhīrapallī*), hamlets (*ghoṣa*), cattle-pens (*vraja*) rich in herds, as well as networks of small villages, at an auspicious moment. The ruler of the earth must systematically ensure that these are equipped with step-wells (*vāpī*) and wells (*kūpa*), adorned with gardens, and surrounded by crop fields (*sasya-kṣetra*). Land fit for crops (*sasyārhī*) is declared to be the essence of villages, towns, and cities; it is the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the supreme source of livelihood. Gārgya, the foremost among speakers, stated that land suitable for crops is the vital artery (*prāṇanāḍī*), and eternal prosperity everywhere arises only from connection with crop-yielding fields. Eminent sages have declared that the fruit of constructing villages and settlements is the protection of life (*prāṇarakṣā*) and the ultimate attainment of human goals (*puruṣārtha*). It brings satisfaction to the gods, the fruit of sacrifices, and the supreme fruit of creation; indeed, it greatly protects the lives of all living beings in the world. It is declared as essential land (*sārabhūmi*) yielding the supreme benefit for living beings; therefore, the king (*mahīpati*) should choose land endowed with auspicious marks and free from defects. Alternatively, he may designate land having very few defects here and there, divided somewhere by a village road (*grāmamārga*) or a town road (*puramārga*). Or he should divide the excellent land in the region by a highway (*mahāmārga*); in the best western part of villages and towns, or in the north, east, or somewhere in the south, he should construct a reservoir (*jalāśaya*) according to the topography of the land. A deep reservoir surrounded by a moat, splendid in the shape of a bow, long in some places, or round and unfathomable. It should be well-protected with sturdy channels, causeways, and pathways, constructed with high embankments and equipped with access roads. It should be especially beautified with water-inlet channels; therefore, near a mountain or on elevated ground, or connected with a large deep pool, he should establish a reservoir that holds stable, abundant water on water-retaining land. He should build it in fertile soil (*sārakṣetra*) or in a place with natural drainage, free from sand and devoid of stones and rocks. The wise ruler should establish a deep water reservoir fitted with flood-gates (*jalapūrargala*) to regulate the water flow. He should build it so that there is no obstruction or danger to villages, towns, surrounding walls, gardens, forts, or threshing floors (*khalakṣetra*). The king (*bhūmipa*) should ensure that there is no fear of water or flooding anywhere; thus he should locate it in the region and test it step by step. Month by month or year by year, repeatedly, the king (*nṛpati*) should station guards there to protect the embankments. Especially during the rainy season (*varṣākāla*), protecting a hundred canals (*kulyā*), stepped wells (*vāpī*), and oblong ponds (*dīrghikā*) is considered to ensure prosperity and safety.

When a reservoir is kept full of water and properly protected in order, the growth of crops and other produce is assured there, bestowing happiness. Freedom from disease, freedom from fear of fire, and supreme happiness prevail; commendable nourishment and protection are provided for bipeds and quadrupeds. Supreme happiness is declared for birds and for creatures such as serpents everywhere, and illness surely does not occur. Water serves as the drinking substance for bipeds, quadrupeds, birds, and serpents everywhere. Supreme happiness is declared and no disease surely arises; water is the drinking substance for bipeds and quadrupeds. This single place of abundant water, designated by Brahmā while creating living beings, is called a reservoir (jalāśaya). Therefore, with all effort, the king who bears the responsibility of protecting his subjects should establish and protect this reservoir systematically. The king should construct two reservoirs, or somewhere a single reservoir, suitable for the village according to the extent of fertile lands. It should be endowed with mountain streams, connected with a large lake, and joined by a forest stream or sometimes a great river. In various regions, especially for villages and towns, he should skillfully arrange places for water distribution in proper order. On the bank of the reservoir, the king should grow trees: vetasa (cane), vaṭa (banyan), and in places rows of kola (jujube) and tuberous plants. Plakṣa, aśvattha, khadira, khādira, tinduka, tintriṇī (tamarind), bhūrja (birch), and veṇu (bamboo); Nimba, kadamba, and whichever other trees are considered valuable—the king should carefully procure these trees at the appropriate time; He should systematically plant them on the bank of the reservoir for securing welfare, or on the lower ground of the bank, or near the channel outlet. Without obstructing the bathing ghat, he should grow trees suitable near the drinking ghat in places, cultivating them skillfully here and there. Likewise, on threshing floors, the king should plant trees such as banyans and others that bring comfort, as well as on the banks of ponds, oblong lakes, and deep pools. The ruler should sequentially nurture densely-shaded trees in pleasure-gardens, parks, and resting grounds. Along main highways near water reservoirs, he should raise trees that diffuse cool breezes and bear blossoms, relieving the fatigue of living beings. In various places suitable for picnics (*vanabhojana*), in temple garden grounds, and in royal gardens, especially around the huts (*uṭaja*) of sages, in military encampments, and in royal resting quarters, as well as in grounds worthy of sacrifices and places for offerings (*bali*), the king should gradually raise densely-shaded trees, trees that bring delight to birds, yield fruits and flowers, alleviate ailments, and are cool and tender. He should plant thornless jackfruit, mango, and juicy mango trees, alongside rows of *punnāga*, *mālatī*, *kunda*, and *champaka*. He should establish them particularly within enclosures, gradually nourishing the trees with the water outflow from reservoirs. Without a water reservoir, happiness is never attained; neither twilight rituals, nor bathing, nor the growth of trees can take place.

Sages have determined that no happiness exists without it; therefore, with all effort, the king, dedicated to protection, should tirelessly construct a deep water reservoir in villages, provinces, or in the midst of forests. He should maintain a sturdy canal with an easily accessible water outflow, having numerous branches and connected to major canals. He should establish it securely together with a water reservoir in a firm and well-constructed manner. Where, for agricultural land, a canal or a water reservoir is nowhere constructed nor established continuously filled with water, There, a canal having a river as its source (nadī-mātṛ-mukhā) should certainly be established; this is declared to be of four kinds by experts in farming methods. The first is river-fed (nadī-mātṛkā), the second is fed by a lake (hradāśritā), another is fed by a reservoir, and one situated along the side of a mountain cliff. Thus, the fourfold canal should be established according to the proportions of the region where, by natural topography, a river or water source is seen in the upper area. There, the canal mouth from the river should be made radiant with a natural discharge, wherever land suitable for cultivation exists in the soil of the region. Generally in that upper portion, whether near or far away, the course of the canal should be constructed by experts in agricultural work. One may begin a canal at a suitable place from an eastward-flowing river, and similarly one should construct a canal from a river flowing westward. Or one may construct it from a river flowing in intermediate directions, or sometimes from a stream flowing into intermediate corners. Land that rises gradually is indeed everywhere preferred; a river-fed canal originating from a river should be well established on proper ground. Gradually traversing diverse and varied terrains, passing from village to village and through forests down to lower ground, One should lead the canal into one's own field for natural prosperity and welfare; its width may be four, five, six, or seven cubits (hasta), Or a width of ten cubits is specified for the canal. Sometimes the water-filled canal originates from a large lake, Or originates from the bed of a river with abundant water; a canal width proportioned to the extent of one's own field is considered best. Thus, it should be designed evenly, but its elevation should suit the terrain. Depth appropriate for proper water flow should be provided everywhere. Crossing a large reservoir or along a central path somewhere below, the king should construct this canal for the welfare of all living beings. He should also construct a canal originating from a mountain spring at the base, leading into his own fields to increase agricultural prosperity. Indeed, one canal full of water, or two canals in some places, or three canals are ordained for the benefit of the fields. In a riverless region, even a canal constructed on sandy ground is determined by agricultural experts to bring happiness and prosperity.

That piece of land which has a continuous flow of water, is free from gravel and stones, forms a good field, and possesses excellent qualities, serves well for the safety of crops. Or, one should direct a canal originating from a lake for the prosperity of one's village, or somewhere in the region for gardens or pleasure-grounds. One should carry out the construction of canals splendid with proper water flow for bathing, drinking, and agricultural work on earth. It is determined by ancient wise sages that water protects life; however, in certain places, the ground destroys or absorbs the canal water. It absorbs or dries up the water itself due to its internal defects. Therefore, such ground should be avoided by experts in canal construction. Saline ground is seen in places across the earth; that land, as well as ground afflicted with soil defects, should be avoided for a canal. Therefore, seeing ground endowed with good qualities, the king should establish the construction of canals in the region for the abundance of crops. In some places two canals should be provided, and in some places three. That construction is declared everywhere according to the suitability of the site. The entry of all canals into reservoir sites is stated in proper order by the great sages who know the scriptures. But in a place lacking a reservoir—whether in a village, town, forest, or woodland—one should direct that canal leading into the fields. Likewise, the wise ruler should construct irrigation channels especially for the growth of crops; down there, a small secondary channel is praised and proves fruit-yielding. Water is considered the very life of living beings as well as crops; therefore, in all lands, for the attainment of general welfare, the king... ...should make the canal—whether river-fed or constructed across different terrains—full of water, get it excavated, and protect it at all times. Unprotected, a canal becomes useless, defective, and devoid of water; hence, by all rulers, the protection of channels is considered a supreme duty. This is declared as righteous duty by truth-perceiving sages, especially concerning step-wells, reservoirs, and wells. Provision of water nourishment is prescribed for agricultural prosperity on earth; in some lands, the presence of water is found in upper strata... ...while in others, the water table is said to be deep below, and in rocky regions, the underground stream disappears. Elsewhere, corrupted by soil defects, the water flow gets lost; therefore, land that is rich in sand and abundant in underground water... ...is judged suitable for step-wells and wells by the experts. In a region where during summer, for crop fields or... ...for gardens, canal water is insufficient, the king should get wells constructed everywhere in that land. He may construct small wells, medium wells, large wells, or step-wells—whether square, circular, or rectangular in shape. He should establish, dig, and maintain them according to prescribed rules.

During the months of Uttarāyaṇa (the sun's northward course), in almost all places... ...water is visible down below or in riverbeds; therefore, the digging of wells and step-wells should take place during Uttarāyaṇa. To ensure a long-lasting and complete water supply, the wise king, guided by an expert in underground water science (dagārgala-vidhi)... ...should undertake the digging of step-wells and wells after first ascertaining the presence of water through trees and soil veins (bhūnāḍī). Having tested the ground, one should undertake the digging at an auspicious moment (su-muhūrta) and favorable astrological lagna; digging in the morning is generally declared to be auspicious. After worshipping Varuna, the lord of waters, Mother Earth (Bhūdevī), and the forest goddess (Vanadevī), especially through offerings (bali). The king should construct a well (kūpa), a stepped well (vāpī), or an oblong pond (dīrghikā) in order, first digging a large pit that is long or square. Or circular in shape, casting the excavated earth far away according to traditional knowledge, until water is encountered. The removal of earth is prescribed to be done by strong workmen and farmers; upon seeing water mixed with sand in wells and reservoirs in order, A foundation at the bottom is prescribed for stability; in sandy ground, it may be made using brick lattice structures, The foundation is instructed to be made with well-baked bricks; however, in a hard ground region when constructing an oblong tank, One should construct the foundation at the bottom using stone blocks; similarly, at the bottom of a well, the foundation is made in due order. By excavating the mud mixed with sand and water, and steadily fortifying it, abundant water is obtained. Finding water there, the king should in due course build upon the foundation in wells and reservoirs using brick masonry. Wise men who know the principles state that constructing wells using bricks and materials mixed with mortar ensures long-lasting durability. Therefore, in all regions, the construction of stepped wells, wells, and other reservoirs should be done with mortar and bricks, as established in the treatises. Daily, construction from the foundation up to the ground surface should be carried out with bricks, and steps should also be built where appropriate. The wise know that the main entrance on the ground level should be built with stones, facing east or west as appropriate for the site. On firm ground at the bank, a platform for a water-lifting wheel (ghaṭī-yantra) should be constructed with stones to allow the discharge of water. Small channels suitable for the land should be constructed on the banks. The various types of water-wheels (ghaṭīyantra) drawn by oxen are considered the best. That water-wheel operated occasionally by means of strong chains using mechanical levers/arms is mediocre, while that driven by human labor is inferior. Driven by the water-wheel, water located below in wells and other sources gradually reaches the bank; this is observed everywhere in the world. That water, conveyed through small channels, is recommended for crop fields.

Therefore, wise men on earth devoted to agricultural pursuits— —whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or others, should skillfully utilize water from ponds, wells, etc., using water-wheels. Pure water stored in reservoirs, flowing through channels from river-fed lands, or originating from lakes, free from impurities, ...should be systematically conveyed to agricultural fields, vegetable plots, and gardens of flowering creepers such as Caṃpaka on the earth. Thus farmers duly accomplish their agricultural purposes in the world. Therefore, farmers having first secured a reservoir site... ...water must indeed be obtained through canals, wells, lakes, and reservoirs on the earth. During the rainy season, rainfall occurs everywhere with certainty, by divine order or through the holy resolves of great sages in every way. O King, water rained down in season by rainclouds should be stored in reservoirs and other water bodies for the attainment of prosperity. It should be preserved with great effort, as agriculture is considered to be rooted in water. Therefore, by rulers everywhere and by other prominent men... ...water obtained during the proper season should everywhere be diligently conserved—so has been declared by the great sage Kāśyapa. Those village-dwelling men who are engaged in agricultural work, free from hypocrisy, envy, and pride, and desirous of mutual welfare, Devoted to cows, land, and the gods, always truthful, intent on helping others, and constantly contented in mind, Having no enemies in the world, dedicated to helping others in their works, adorned with affection for four-legged animals, and skilled in prudence, Skilled in accounting, pure, devoted to cleanliness, observant of daily duties, and performing proper hospitality to guests in due time, Free from torpor and laziness, devoid of lust and anger, sharing mutual affection, and devoted to cooperative work, Such men are declared to be noble and of auspicious sight, serving as protectors of the banks of water reservoirs, canals, and similar structures. Solely intent on cow protection, possessing the trust of the king, blessed with sons, grandsons, fathers-in-law, and brothers, Whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras who live by agriculture, or those born of mixed castes, hunters, and other men on earth, Those who are fond of hunting, those regarded as cowherds, those known as goat-herds, and all other agriculturalists, All these men in the world, in every region and in all ways, endowed with mutual affection, are consecrated to the welfare of the public. By the king's order, under the guidance of village leaders and community elders, people should be instructed in their respective callings, being respectful of public opinion and compassionate. Dedicated to the sacred task named the preservation of their respective livelihoods, these holy men are declared to act for the benefit of all living creatures. Among them, those Brāhmaṇas who are pure, devoted to truth and righteousness, compassionate, versed in ethics, and adorned with repentance for shortcomings, They should be inflictors of appropriate punishment, dedicated to the work of all-round protection, eager to execute the king's orders, and adorned with many noble virtues.

One who desires prosperity should appoint such persons as village headmen (*grāmādhipati*), either for a single village or for a cluster of villages in certain regions. Those who maintain stability in matters of justice and injustice and establish righteousness (*dharma*) are indeed proclaimed as promoters and supporters of agricultural operations. Thus, kings, *Kṣatriyas*, wealthy people, and *Vaiśyas* should render assistance in agricultural work for the general welfare of the world. Assisting agriculture is declared to be righteous, glorious, and conducive to longevity; therefore, kings, *Kṣatriyas*, *Brāhmaṇas*, and *Vaiśyas* [should offer such aid]. Even *Śūdras*, according to their capability, gain immense benefit by assisting agriculture through donations of various types of seeds and cattle. Great sages say that donating land brings immense religious merit in the world, as does digging irrigation canals (*kulyā*) or protecting crop fields. Great merit is attained by supporting agriculture through constructing water reservoirs, especially step-wells (*vāpī*), or establishing free food halls (*anna-śālā*). Providing assistance according to one's power by protecting cows and especially *Brāhmaṇas* is declared to yield great fruit. Therefore, compassionate men in all regions [should appoint] guards for village protection and guards for embankment protection. Having deployed guards everywhere, especially in key places, driving away thieves and punishing those liable for punishment in due order, Men who ensure the maintenance of *dharma*, supreme happiness, and the protection of life are praised even by the gods. That person in whom truthfulness, charity, forgiveness, good character, non-cruelty, austerity, and compassion are all observed should be appointed to authority. Rulers should duly assign village lordship in the village judicial assembly (*grāma-nyāya-sabhā*) and promote agricultural methods. Great sages state that prosperity flourishes under such authority; in the absence of a *Brāhmaṇa*, a *Kṣatriya* or a *Vaiśya* may be appointed. He should be employed there for the welfare of the subjects; everywhere the authority of the sages leads to prosperity and victory. But the skill of agriculture in this world is sometimes found even among Shudras. Such a Shudra should be rich in virtues and devoted to Brahmins. He should have faith in the scriptures, know proper respect, serve the righteous, be intelligent, understand seasonal timings, act beneficially, and be fond of well-being. He must be humble, and his agricultural practical knowledge deserves praise. Generally in all villages, the working servants are declared to be Shudras. They alone should be engaged in agricultural labour, not other castes. Vaishyas and Kshatriyas, endowed with good qualities and sharp intellects, Should be appointed by rulers in accounting and protective duties, while Brahmins should always be appointed in matters of state policy and law. In tasks of protecting cattle, guarding the subjects, punishing thieves and criminals, and preserving water reservoirs, In protecting temples, especially in agricultural work, as well as in other rural affairs and royal duties, Brahmins, Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras—all possessing firm intellect—should all be suitably employed everywhere; then it conduces to overall welfare.

Then, for the province and especially for the whole nation, supreme happiness and harmony arise through unity of purpose. "Let unanimity of voice and unity of mind be observed constantly even among tiny insects"—so was declared here by the silent sage Bhargava. Therefore, whether in a village, a district, a town, or in fort planning, all resident people should shed bad traits like envy. In protecting dams and bridges, protecting roads, protecting crops, protecting towns and villages, and protecting parks and gardens, In protecting the populace, in protecting cattle, in upholding dharma, and in safeguarding the administration of justice, And whatever other various forms of protection have been declared by the great sages, in all those protective duties, all residents of villages and towns must cooperate. Showing individual respect is supreme, commended, and enjoined by the scriptures. In whatever village or kingdom a palace/residence for the king is not established, in that region, especially for the protection of the subjects, a minister, a member of the royal family, or a virtuous representative, supported by wealth and an army, should take up residence, grant what is requested by the subjects, and greatly protect them from calamities. He should arrange for the livelihood of the people through various means, including Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and those born of mixed castes. And whichever other men live in villages and other localities in the world, devoted to their own duties, become happy and famous. Having attained supreme joy, along with their families and herds of cattle, they shine brightly everywhere in various regions. All men who obey the king's commands, respect the Śrutis and Smṛtis, are dedicated to helping others, and are free from fear, being free from mental and physical diseases, performing good deeds, and serving the virtuous, shine brightly in various lands. For all of them, the occupation of agriculture (kṛṣi-vṛtti) is eternal, auspicious, bestowing prosperity, and commendable when conducted according to justice. Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, even while engaged in their own duties, are fit for agricultural work; indeed, they know it to be highly praised by the wise. Sages endowed with divine vision praise agricultural work as the foundation of sacrifices and the bestower of life upon living beings. Having obtained crop fields—whether granted by the king or purchased by oneself—people should be industrious and respectful toward agricultural work. They are considered bringers of delight to the gods and sages; among all forms of wealth, agriculture alone is the ultimate wealth. It is declared to be unseizable by others, praised by all, yields great fruit, pleases the gods, and bestows pure substances. It removes dependence, constantly brings the play of prosperity (Lakṣmī), and gives life and sustenance to guests, gods, and one's own family. Agricultural work, which bestows various kinds of happiness, is praised; therefore, any occupation other than this is bound by dependence on others.

Even the blameless livelihood of virtuous people (in other professions) is criticized by seers of truth; therefore, a man endowed with good virtues should, through his own effort, engage in agriculture. Whether proficient in Vedic studies, engaged in protection (Kshatriyas), involved in trade (Vaishyas), Shudras, or even those of mixed castes, If they are devoted to truth, rich in compassion, and earnestly committed to taking up agriculture, their livelihood is indeed highly respected by holy men and even by the gods. One should diligently protect the practice of agriculture, which delights all the gods and provides sustenance to all living beings. Great sages consider the practice of agriculture worthy of undertaking in forests, inhabited regions, countryside, fields, villages, and on mountain slopes. Ancient sages, who wished well for all living creatures, themselves performed agricultural work in the courtyard grounds of their hermitages. From then on, agricultural work was systematically spread across all regions by sharp-minded scholars and gradually became fruitful everywhere. Therefore, this practice of agriculture should be cultivated by all eminent men of refined intellect for the sake of everlasting joy. Kashyapa advises: An intelligent person, expert in farming and foremost among those who know the characteristics of soil, should cheerfully begin agricultural operations at an auspicious hour. To achieve fruitfulness, he should engage in farming after contemplating the Trinity and remembering Goddess Earth and Goddess Dhanya (Grain) in a pure mind. Having worshipped them with devotion, he should prepare to collect materials, after plastering the cow-shed or cattle station with cow-dung. Especially splendid with decorations such as fragrant flowers, and posts made from the strong timber of tinduka, tinisha, or sarja trees. Having erected cattle-tethering posts adorned with chains, and having decorated that area with perfumes, kumkuma, and blossoms; Having performed circumambulation, the wise person should cause cows to graze in that spot, letting cows endowed with auspicious marks roam around there. As well as white-bodied bulls endowed with auspicious marks, having horn-tips covered in gold and silver, decorated with perfumes and ornaments; He should furnish that cattle-pen area at an auspicious hour with grasses, young sprouts, straw, and auspicious water vessels. Or having bought white bulls esteemed for their good characteristics, or cows or buffaloes, the learned person should tie them there. Then, plows equipped with ropes and all their essential parts and plow-shafts, crafted from solid hardwood; Placing them in an auspicious place, adorned especially with fragrant mango leaves, flowers, sandalwood paste, and kumkuma; Amid auspicious chants, he should worship the Goddess of Grain, as well as the Earth Goddess, Lakshmi, Vani, Gauri, and Indra; And having especially worshipped Varuna and Kubera, the expert should proceed to his own field along with the bulls. Equipped with fine plows, at an auspicious hour and ascendant, he should first initiate plowing in the auspicious north-eastern corner. Or in the south-eastern or western part at an appropriate spot, filling it with water in due order for thorough plowing.

The expert in agricultural operations should carry out the first plowing of the soil in his own field using a plow yoked to bulls. In this manner, having plowed that field four or five times with the plow for six days or longer; Having cleared away clods, sticks, and other debris, he should apply cow dung, goat manure, or organic fertilizer there to enrich the soil. Digging tools, pegs, small blades/knives, daggers, and small knives suitable for agriculture are indeed prescribed in the treatises on materials (*dravya-śāstra*). The farmer should properly bring all these along with sickles and harvesting tools; whenever and wherever the first rainfall is seen on the land in any region, then the great sages knowledgeable in food declare ploughing the land to be best, after filling one's own land with water through the mouth of the channel (*kulyā*). Tilling of the soil at the time suitable for crops is declared by the sage; therefore, in all regions, according to the season suitable for agriculture, and following the advice of friends, one expert in farm work should wisely undertake the initial ploughing of the land under auspicious omens and favorable astrological moments. Even before furrowing the land, farmers knowledgeable in signs should perform the worship of the plough and other implements, and especially of the bulls and oxen. Worship of the farm field or soil yields rich fruits when performed with pure water, fragrant substances like sandalwood, and by offering lighted lamps. [Prayer:] "O Goddess Earth (*Bhūmidevi*), salutations to you, O all-enduring Mother! I am now commencing the agricultural work; be pleased with me, O virtuous one! Whatever ploughing, striking, or digging is done upon you by me, O Goddess, forgive it all and grant me a great harvest! You alone are celebrated as the mother of all living creatures in this world; therefore, O Earth Goddess, be gracious and bestow immeasurable produce upon the land!" Having thus praised and prayed to Goddess Earth, the beloved of Viṣṇu, the farmer should circumambulate her with respectful bows. Also offering prayers to the directional deities (*dig-deva*), the guardian spirits, and the life-bestowing Sun, he should make an auspicious beginning to the ritual of ploughing the earth. O son of Surabhi, possessor of great strength, king of bulls of boundless lustre, sinless one! Render assistance to me in the work of plowing the land. Today I worship you with fragrant garlands, flowers, and other offerings. May you bestow success upon me, O practitioner of righteousness; abundant welfare be unto you! I nourish you with devotion through grass, young fodder, and water. By the grace of Shankara, may you always grant fruitfulness to me. Continually producing offspring equal to you in strength, vigor, and splendor, adorn my cattle-shed; I nourish you with deep respect. O king of bulls, you alone bring about the increase of wealth, grains, and prosperity here. You are the very embodiment of Dharma on earth, and therefore I nourish you.

So that my sacrifices to the gods (*deva-yajna*) and living beings (*bhuta-yajna*) become fruitful, show mercy to me and forgive my offenses. Having thus prayed to and especially worshipped the bull, work should be assigned only to the extent that they do not become weary or exhausted from fatigue. For whatever causes distress to their mind surely leads to failure. Therefore, one should never employ exhausted bulls in agricultural work; at that time, worship of the cows/bulls is praised, so say the best of sages. Cows and bulls that shine with auspicious characteristics are said to bring good fortune to their owners and bestow well-being upon the country. Such bulls, which increase prosperity, are suitable for agricultural work; those with white bodies, slightly tall stature, and beautiful eyes— —and possessing a deep roar, belong to the Brāhmaṇa class. Those with reddish bodies, very tall height, and deep roars— —and endowed with vigor and strength, are bulls of the Kṣatriya class. Those marked with white and red spots and adorned with circular patterns— —neither very tall nor very short, belong to the Vaiśya class. Those with thin bodies, not very tall, and driven by fits of anger— —and obedient/gentle, are bulls of the Śūद्र class. All these kinds of bulls are praised and suitable for agricultural work. A pair of bull's horns that is neither too long nor thin is auspicious; mutually symmetrical horns of a bull are commended. The hooves of bulls should not be thin nor overly long; those that are symmetrical and firm are considered praiseworthy. An auspicious gait and a long tail are praised in bulls, as is the capacity to carry loads while being neither too stout nor lean. Tranquillity or cheerfulness during work is the supreme quality of bulls. A bull having white color on its hooves, horns, forehead, and tail— —and adorned with diverse colors promotes prosperity. Those that are pleasing, cheerful, and radiant with auspicious colors— —and possessed of auspicious whorls of hair, grant growth of wealth and grain. Those covered with a line of fine hair and possessing deep roars— —and endowed with pleasing eyes, are regarded as auspicious. Those of red color with large horns, but devoid of vigor and strength, [are inferior]. Bulls that stumble while running fast, are overcome by anger and sleep, have emaciated bodies, are smoky-colored, or eat excessively [are inferior and should be avoided]. Bulls that are discolored, extremely low-statured, rough-bodied, and possess cruel/sharp hooves are the worst among bulls and must be avoided. Bulls possessing an entirely white body or a reddish body are declared to bring good fortune and increase wealth, grain, and prosperity. Bulls free of defects, endowed with good qualities, and born of a pure breed should especially be acquired by farmers for achieving security and success. Cows and buffaloes possessing auspicious characteristics are likewise considered suitable, and female buffaloes yielding abundant milk should be protected by farmers.

Sheep and goats in many ways yield fruits for agricultural work, as tested and advised by the learned through traditional teachings. Those seeking auspiciousness should carefully protect bulls and other animals verified to be free from defects, for the sake of success in agriculture. They should be nourished at the proper times with wholesome food and protected daily from diseases through caring attention and fondness. The wise person should designate a cattle-pen area that promotes their health; indeed, excellent bulls are the primary support in agricultural work. Therefore, cows born of good lineage in particular should be maintained by farmers everywhere, in villages as well as in towns. Hundreds of cows endowed with auspicious marks should be reared by farmers in villages and in towns. Through providing straw, grass, water, etc., along with pampering and extensive protection, the attainment of *dharma*, *kama*, and *artha* comes from rearing cows. In that land where a thousand cows are lovingly maintained, there is alleviation of diseases and protection of children, the elderly, and others. In those lands rain falls without a doubt; through the protection and gifting of cows, the highest satisfaction of the gods is attained. Thus Bhargava stated that this brings welfare to the subjects; therefore, with all effort, farmers should protect the herds of cattle. They should protect them near the borders of forests, inside the village, and everywhere—by themselves, through their servants, and especially by cowherds. Annual worship of cows at an auspicious time is specifically recommended, as is daily worship of them at the end of the day with sandalwood paste, flowers, and other offerings. This is declared in all scriptures to bring fame and auspiciousness, bestowing good offspring upon men as well as the fruits of the three goals of life (dharma, artha, and kāma). During the summer season at midday, the wise person should keep and protect them—the cows, goats, bulls, and other working animals—in shady areas. During cold seasons, they should be well protected in the cattle-shed by serving wholesome food and care, for the welfare and prosperity of the king and his family. Protecting cattle is declared a righteous duty for kings; safeguarding them from thieves and wild beasts, as well as caring for them, is declared to bring great rewards, especially in agricultural work. Wise people everywhere in the world who understand the sequence of agricultural tasks should maintain bulls, buffaloes, cows, servants, and attendants. [Missing text] ... having nourished those who know their duties, they should carry out agriculture planned in the fields. They should gradually enhance the various capabilities of the fields; here, examining the season first is prescribed as the principal rule. In the lands of Kaśmīra, Vaṅga, Nepāla, Pañcāla, Kosala, Kuru, Virāṭa, and Avanti, in Mālava, Śaka country, Sindhu-Sauvīra lands, or in Śūrasena, Avanti, Cedi, Koṅkaṇa, Āndhra, and other regions, whenever rainfall occurs, agricultural work is recommended.

Where, during summer and other seasons, water comes by way of rivers, canals, etc., and is lifted into the fields, agricultural work is then praised. Where from deep reservoirs, channels, and small canals, wherever water is lifted, agriculture is auspicious there. Observing the water flow from rain clouds, deep water reservoirs, and the abundance of canal water, the wise farmer should methodically plan farming based on the land's resources on earth. Fields in the world are divided into two types according to their natural character—along riverbanks, in villages, and inside forests, on mountain slopes, and on uneven low and elevated grounds. Among these, the first, śāli (paddy) land, is declared supreme by the sages. The second type, āḍhaka (pulse) land, is medium yet fruitful. Śāli land, however, is naturally abundant in water. It is known for complete mud and extremely soft soil, intertwined with major and minor canals and branches flowing with water. It is surrounded on all sides by small protective mud dikes, situated near threshing floors or near village residential areas. The condition of śāli-land is determined by the alignment of the fields, being low-lying in some places towards the east and in others towards the west. Sometimes it is low-lying on the south, or has low ground towards the north; occasionally it is mostly level with water channels directed to receive water. From another field, there is sometimes a stream of water fit to enter the field's surface; thus the various characteristics of śāli-land are defined. From the first plowing up to the production of grain on this earth, śāli-land well-supplied with water is renowned for yielding complete harvest. The second type of land, elevated ground situated near village dwelling sites, at forest fringes, or on banks, is designated as āḍhaka-land (for pulse crops). Sustained even by small drops of water, it promotes the growth of chickpea (caṇaka) and pigeon pea (āḍhaka); constructing water channels for it is not prescribed. It generally becomes suitable for plowing with a small sprinkling of water, requiring only slight absorption of water at the time of sowing seeds. Thus, irrigation at the appropriate time gives life to the seeds; land endowed with such qualities is described as āḍhaka-ground. Here, the sage explains the various methods of seed collection suitable for farmers regarding both śāli-land and āḍhaka-land. Formerly, when requested, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, created various seeds here on earth and then reflected upon the matter. Understanding his intention, the glorious Earth Goddess joyfully spoke to the Creator (Brahmā) for securing the happiness of living beings. "O Creator, indeed these various seeds created by you were deposited in me with due respect without delay." The seeds will surely sprout without any doubt, through the abundance of your grace, and especially that of Vasava (Indra). Every year rainfall from clouds will regularly occur, and people everywhere will receive rain in due season. Having sown seeds especially in fertile fields, people will certainly reap full benefits, remaining well-nourished and joyful.

Experts in agriculture will flourish in various lands on earth; divine satisfaction will be matchless, and sacrifices (yajñas) will prosper. Gratifying the subjects and guests with food, and satisfying cows and other animals at the proper time, renders the sacrifice to all beings (bhūtayajña) fruitful. Thus requested by Goddess Medinī (Earth), the lotus-seated Brahmā uttered the words "So be it," granting benefit to all living beings. From that time onward, all kinds of seeds in the world are preserved by sharp-minded humans who know the art of agriculture. The great sages specified rice (*śāli*) and similar grains as the first category, pulses like pigeon pea (*āḍhakī*) as the second, and the group of vegetables (*śāka*) as the third. The category of creepers and flowers is stated as the fourth; thus agriculture in this world is determined to be fourfold. It yields fruits and bestows nourishment especially upon human beings, generating contentment in all seasons and giving delight to the gods. It gives life to animals like cows, bulls, camels, horses, and elephants (*kumbhin*); indeed, it was taught on earth by eminent yogis such as Nārada. Excellent kings carried out agricultural operations with devotion in their respective lands, and it was maintained by their servants. From then on, agriculture suited to the season was undertaken in good fields in many ways by noble Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdrās, and others. Agricultural work was thus commenced, with seed declared as its primary element; therefore, by the wise on earth who are foremost among agricultural experts— —a collection of seeds must definitely be made systematically; I shall now list the names of the seeds in sequence for success here. Paddy is threefold—śāli etc., kalama etc., and ṣaṣṭika etc.; it is classified by agricultural experts according to taste, color, variety, and other characteristics. Kalama grains are somewhat dense, highly flavorful, and bright, whereas ṣaṣṭिका grains were created lacking in taste by the lotus-born Lord (Brahmā). Śāli-vrīhi rice is declared by experts to have twenty-six varieties, depending on the variations in soil in different regions. Sowing of seeds must be performed unslothfully at the right time; therefore, preserving them with utmost effort is advised. [The varieties are] śweta-śāli, rakta-śāli, sthūla-śāli, long dīrgha-śāli of delicious taste, and white-colored kalama, Red-colored kalama, thick-bodied kalama, long-shaped kalama, and the vrīhi known as hemākhya-śambaka, Brown śambaka, another śambaka red in color, and black śambaka of a different form considered exceedingly flavorful, Śuka-vrīhi, another large-bodied vrīhi variety, ghana-vrīhi, and palaśa-vrīhi rich in sap/flavor, Exceedingly sweet vrīhi, another called phala-vrīhi, drākṣā-vrīhi, and wild nīvāra of white and black varieties, Two barley-shaped vrīhi varieties (white and black), a large-grained one, and another called samara-vrīhi which yields abundant quantities, Kala-vrīhi which is supreme and highly nourishing, sita-vrīhi, yellow-colored vrīhi, and the vrīhi that cures indigestion. Thus twenty-six varieties of grain crops have been listed; next, the systematic preservation of all these seeds is described. Preserving well-matured seeds dried in sunlight, whether at the threshing floor or at home, is paramount and brings auspicious prosperity.

Seeds should be protected by rulers or distributed at the proper time; the stock of seeds is the highest asset and the primary wealth of agriculture. It pleases men and gods alike and is worthy of being offered as gifts; therefore, proper preservation of seeds by farmers is recommended. These seeds yield complete fruit within three or four months on land. Some yield fruit in five months, some here in six months, and some progressively in seven or eight months in certain places. The great sages have determined that these yield fully ripened fruit; therefore, in one's own region and fields, according to favorable water drainage, The commencement of agricultural activities for rice (*sali*) and other crops brings success and happiness, following the traditional order of ancestral practices in some places. Agricultural work is praised when carried out on earth in accordance with place and time, following the onset of clouds and the natural flow of water. Agriculture is declared to bring fruit to kings, subjects, cows, and even insects in due order. Agricultural work is certainly the bestower of happiness to all living beings. Likewise, seeds of *adhaka* (pigeon pea) and *masha* (black gram) in order, As well as seeds of *mudga* (mung bean), *chanaka* (chickpea), and especially *godhuma* (wheat), *tila* (sesame), *kiraka*, and *kodrava* (kodo millet) in certain places, Of *yavara* (barley), *kuluttha* (horse gram), *shyama*, *krishnasari*, and *ikshu* (sugarcane) such as *pundra*, categorized by varieties and juice properties, The hot-natured seeds (*ushna-bijaka*) of various divided grains, as well as seeds of *jiraka* (cumin), *sarshapa* (mustard), and *marichi* (black pepper), And of *tula* (cotton) and *eranda* (castor) to be sown in suitable places—the preservation of all these seeds brings happiness. Likewise, the seeds of *patolika* (pointed gourd) and *vartaka* (eggplant), as well as *jatika*, *rashijatika*, *vallika* (creepers), and *vanavallika* (wild creepers), And various juice-filled *chavaka* are described, as well as diverse vegetables distinguished by color, taste, and variety. Seeds of *kushmanda* (ash gourd) and *kalata* take various forms; so too seeds of *kustumburu* (coriander), *kata*, and *dhanyaka* in certain places. The preservation of seeds of *haridra* (turmeric), *shunshti* (dry ginger), *surana* (elephant foot yam), tubers, and *shakuta* is auspicious. The preservation of seeds/shoots of rasāka and especially plantains should be carried out by experts in agriculture. The preservation of seeds of cardamom (elā), grapes (drākṣā), vetiver (nalada), juice-rich betel vine (nāgavallī), and betel nuts (pūga and kramuka) is auspicious. They should preserve the seeds of jasmine (mallikā), yellow-flowered plants, kunda, atimuktā, and occasionally cāmpeya (champaka). Likewise, [seeds] of śigru (drumstick), bhūrja (birch), karañja, and sometimes śamī, naktamāla, and trees called devadāru (cedar)... ...and of vibhītaka, priyaṅgu, āmalaka trees, piṇḍīṭaka, nimba (neem), and occasionally likuca trees. Similarly, [seeds] of śirīṣa, aśoka, pomegranate (dāḍima), śrīparṇī, tamāla, and the trees known as sindhuvāra... ...and of kapittha (wood-apple), jambū (rose-apple), and trees called saptaparṇa—seed preservation must be carried out by farmers for their prosperity.

Udumbara (fig), caladala (peepal), tiniśa, pāribhadraka, palāśa, madhūka, vaṭa (banyan), plakṣa, rasālaka... ...tinduka, tilaka, nīpa, arjuna, sarjaka, badara (jujube), pīlu trees, jambīra (lime), and punnāga trees... ...bamboo (vaṁśa), various kāśa grasses, and the tree known as mātuluṅga (citron)—thus various trees with leaves, flowers, and fruits... ...which yield fruit for human beings and especially for birds, such as the great trees like vaṭa and others that have been described... For all of these, the preservation of seeds is beneficial, especially when they are fully ripe and dried in the sun. The seed lineage must be preserved by farmers in various vessels, in heaps of straw, and in pots. The seed stock should not be allowed to be spoiled by hares, mice, or cats, nor by water droplets, wind, rain, and the like. The seed stock should be protected at home and at the threshing floor in such a manner that it is not ruined by various other defects. Preservation of excellent seeds out of a sense of duty is declared by eminent sages for the welfare of farmers. [This applies to] seeds of rice (śāli) and vegetables, as well as seeds of trees and seed-tubers of root crops. People skilled in farming—whether Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, or those of mixed castes—having bought or collected seeds in the world, [Should sow them] with care and skill in their own fields situated in their own region, especially in lands of various forms plowed by bulls. At the proper time, after watering or nurturing them, they should plant them systematically according to the rules of seed-sowing. Experts in the scriptures have described various methods of seed-sowing; in some places, plowing is done on rice lands using auspicious bulls. Therefore, it is prescribed that the initial growth of these seeds of paddy (vrīhi) varieties and root crops should first take place on dry ground. Thus it is instructed by experts in agriculture; [they may be grown] in wetland, or in a dry field distinct from it, or in a well-watered clean plot. Having systematically had the earth plowed with bulls, various fields become suitable for seed-sowing. After having the soil prepared and leveled, or for planting sprouts, they should arrange the ground with skill according to their capacity, as suitable for the site. [Whether] in pleasure-gardens, groves, royal gardens, or in sites located outside or inside a village or city. Plowing the soil with bulls, leveling with hoes and similar tools, and smoothing fields with clod-breakers etc., is prescribed. The sequence of furrows in fields for sowing seeds has been prescribed by experts, along with agricultural procedures, and in certain cases, digging alone is specified. One should prepare a pit for planting tubers and bulbs, as well as for plantain and other creeping plants and trees that have been described. Experts in agriculture recommend various techniques for them—properly planting their seed-sprouts, planting tubers, or propagating via creepers.

Sages who perceive the truth state that planting at the right time in a well-leveled, fertile field prepared with crushed soil yields fruitful results. Therefore, plowing the land is recommended in *śāli*-rice fields, creeper plots, land suitable for growing vegetables, gardens, and tree-plantation sites. The agricultural expert should plan plowing, pit digging, furrows, and line layouts according to the suitability of each specific field. The wise cultivator should recommend sowing seeds in a place that has been drained of excess irrigation and dried gradually by the rays of the sun. Similarly, these methods apply to planting creepers, planting trees, placing banana tubers, and planting sprouts. All agricultural operations, beginning with land plowing, should be executed with sound reasoning and according to traditional teachings to achieve successful yields. In regions such as Kosala, which are abundant in river water, the cultivation of *śāli* rice and other grain crops is considered supreme. Thus it has been specified by sages; therefore, intelligent farmers who are determined to secure abundant yields of *kalama* and *vrīhi* rice should practice it. Water from reservoirs, rivers, or deep pools should be conveyed into crop fields through canal outlets at the proper time as instructed. First filling the field with water, plowing with bulls is prescribed thereafter; then, O men, the crop fields become full of water. Plowing starting from the north-eastern direction (Iśāna/Śāṁkara) or in some places towards the east or west is considered auspicious. One should order the systematic uprooting of the dense clusters of rice (śāli) seedlings grown earlier in a separate plot. Having bundled those clusters of seedlings, when the paddy field full of water and mud has softened after plowing, and after carefully enriching the soil with particles of goat dung, cow dung, and creepers or vines, the laborers should plant them row by row on leveled ground; thereafter, only a small amount of water should be maintained in that field. A drainage route for excess water should be constructed especially so that the young crop shoots are not destroyed. Their protection should be carried out accordingly, as this effort is known to yield fruit; thus the orderly planting of clusters of seedlings is recommended. Wherever seedlings have been destroyed due to rain or various other causes, the wise farmer should diligently in that area arrange for the replanting of fresh seedlings to ensure fruitfulness, whether in village fields, wild areas, or other plots. On elevated ground, one, two, three, four, or five householders together, utilizing ten or twenty times more bulls in rows of yokes, plowing the crop lands all at once by villagers in unity with numerous pairs of oxen promotes the growth of crops. Simultaneous sowing of seeds is declared to be fruitful, especially in rice fields filled with mud and water.

Whether in a village, town, or forest tract, when the rice seedlings are planted after draining water through channels, upon the reduction of excess water, the row of rice seed-sprouts planted in the soil across multiple plots thrives properly. Having passed seventeen days, the plant in the ploughed land takes root and is ordained by Brahma to grow. Then appears the auspicious emergence of fresh outer leaves, possessing a charming lustre like that seen on the feathers of parrots. Adorned with that radiance, it shines like a young maiden reaching youth; thus passes the first month in the paddy field. Gradually, the growth of leaves of varieties such as Kalama is seen, along with all-round sprouting equal in beauty. Absorbing water daily, the crop becomes capable of yielding fruit; around this time, weeds and wild grasses appear in the crop fields. These weeds thrive in muddy water and are declared by the best of sages to be the real enemies of the crop. Therefore, farmers should carefully and skillfully remove weeds, Munja grass, and other harmful elements from the land. It is proper to sever at the root all weeds like Munja that cause reduction in yield and impair crop growth. Filling the paddy fields with water, an expert farmer should systematically clear out the weeds row by row. The daily removal of these enemy weeds across all crop fields by hired labor is highly recommended. When these enemy weeds are carefully held in check (or removed) by the farmers, the Sali rice crop shines with splendour and vigorous growth. In the second month, the growth of Sali rice continues steadily; if any weed enemies should still appear then, their diligent removal from the fields is said to bring great yields for all kinds of crops. For White Sali, Red Sali, Kalama, and the various other types of grain previously described, agricultural operations are indeed similar: first comes the ploughing of the land, followed by sowing the seed-sprouts. In clearing out weeds and sticks, that work should be done with care, along with complete watering and protection of the śāli paddy. Although agricultural experts deem these tasks similar in nature and practice, nevertheless, varieties of rice such as śāli, śaṁvā, and kalama on the lands... ...differ by species and properties; some yield fruit in three months, some in four months, and others in five months. Still others yield fruit in six months or even longer. Therefore, understanding the sequence of the emergence of grain ears on the land, farmers should irrigate them accordingly; this is prescribed by agricultural experts in every region and everywhere. When the cluster of grain ears along the crop rows is seen gradually filled with milky grain (kṣīragarbha), dense, and slightly bent down, then protecting that mass of grain ears from birds like parrots is specified as equally vital across all regions. Thus, the row of grain ears filled with milky sap inside gradually solidifies, and that core substance matures into rice grains (taṇḍula).

Until that stage, filling the fields with water is declared beneficial and productive; otherwise, there will be a lack of yield. Therefore, observing the sequence of milk development and stage intervals, at that time, to enhance the milky growth at the root of the crops, farmers should gradually regulate water drainage, or irrigate with water from rivers and reservoirs where appropriate. Diligent watering from lakes, wells, and other sources at that time is declared fruitful for securing the well-being of all creatures. By the boon of Earth and the intention of Brahmā, various seeds sown in the crop fields, grow step by step on the soil and become fruit-bearing, shining on the surface of the earth according to their inherent nature. Protecting the crop from rats, locusts, harmful insects, parrots, and other destructive living creatures is known to yield great rewards. Loving and affectionate towards one another, the village farmers should determine the maturity of crops like *kalama* paddy from their appearance. Based on direct experience, the strength of the seeds, and the quality of the land, fully ripe crops like *shali* rice should be protected by the farm hands. Honored with circumambulations and auspicious rites, when the ears of grain ripen in due order upon the stalks, at that specific stage and time, watering should no longer be done; so it has been instructed by the foremost knowers of agricultural science. This procedure for all *shali* paddy fields has been declared by the wise; therefore, when the paddy ears reach maturity, farmers— —should tirelessly protect them from various types of damage. Thus, when the collection of paddy ears matures at the tips of the leaves, the line of paddy stalks along with their ear-heads bends down toward the earth; seeing them thus fallen, for up to twenty days, one should inspect and guard the field, either through servants or by oneself. Then, when the proper time arrives for the paddy stalks, which are fully ripe and tinged with a golden color, the cutting of those stalks should be done by the farmers using sickles (*shaṅkulā*). Farmers should also have the array of stalks of the *kalama* crop harvested by groups of dependents and other laborers. Either all at once or daily, through mutual cooperation, cutting the stalks of *shali* and other paddy crops brings good results. Whether affected or unaffected by rains, thieves, or other factors, the harvesting of the various crops should be carried out accordingly. The farmers, along with their servants and attendants, should transport and place the cut paddy stalks with their ear-heads onto the threshing floor (*khala-bhūmi*). Keeping and guarding them on the threshing floor for three to five days is commended and said to yield great benefit. By threshing the smooth-topped, fully ripe stalks of paddy on the threshing floor, the grains are separated from the ear-heads. The fallen grain shines pure like a string of strung gems.

When the tips of the paddy stalks are again threshed diligently, Or by the trampling of the feet of bulls and buffaloes, the remaining grain falls down below. Having thus threshed the rows of paddy stalks on the threshing floor, farmers should heap up the heavy, solid, separated grains. The farmers should diligently heap up the lighter and softer grains separately, winnowing them using winnowing baskets, wind, and fanning. Then, after drying them in the sun, the wise man should clean them. He should successively set aside one share for the gods and one for the king, As well as one share for a learned Śrotriya scholar. After paying dues or providing support for his dependents and servants in suitable places, He should store the remaining heap of grain in his own home, carefully protecting it against dampness, hardness, and spoilage through appropriate means. Storage may be in well-baked earthen pots or, in some places, in bins constructed from strong wood, Or in smeared containers woven with strong rope according to regional custom; or he may construct a storage pit in firm ground. In such a pit fitted with steps, he should store paddy and other grains, protecting them skillfully from water, thieves, and parrots, As well as keeping them safe from mice and harmful creatures. This is the supreme method for preserving kalama and vrīhi paddies and grains. The preservation of seeds dried thoroughly in the sun has likewise been prescribed in this manner by excellent farmers. When the heap of grain has thus been brought home by the farmers, the stalks of grain, paddy, etc., dried in the sun, And crushed by the hooves of cattle into a soft-fibered mass, should be gathered and stored in one's house or cattle shed. Having stored it, special care should be taken to protect the straw, which serves as fodder for cows, bulls, and buffaloes in appropriate places. The sustenance of buffaloes, goats, and sometimes deer by means of these bundles of straw is established in the scriptures. Therefore, in all regions, wise farmers engage in the noble work of preserving human life through grains and agricultural produce. By protecting the lives of four-legged animals with crop stalks and straw, those who make efforts according to prescribed rules attain great joy. Following the teachings of the noble, local customary traditions, and personal experience combined with reasoning, farmers remain devoted to agricultural pursuits. Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, mixed castes, and all others derive wealth from the earth in the form of harvested heaps of grain. Storing the harvested grain in the best part of their house during an auspicious hour and moment, they worship Dhānyalakṣmī (goddess of grain) and Dhanalakṣmī (goddess of wealth). Offering perfumes, flowers, and pure items prescribed by scripture, they feed Brāhmaṇas and present them with auspicious gifts (dakṣiṇā).

Having attained fame, happiness, supreme wealth on earth, divine favor, good sons, and wives, Together with grandchildren and family, they continuously rejoice and prosper, having successfully accomplished agricultural work in various śāli (rice) fields. People carry out farming skillfully in their own country, in forest lands, in villages, in fertile fields, or on high grounds (sthalī). By undertaking a second agricultural crop in fertile fields with perennial water supply, noble farmers obtain abundant harvests. Thus, double cropping every year in various types of fields is praised everywhere as highly fruitful. By applying goat dung, cow dung, and green manures such as kalatā to enhance field fertility, a second cropping cycle is recommended. Proper, step-by-step agricultural operations are declared fruitful when accompanied by daily inspection and care of the śāli fields. By following a systematic sequence of farming and taking care of cows and livestock, peaceful farmers obtain great prosperity and rewards. Therefore, those who know the procedures of agriculture, speaking sweetly and in a friendly manner, should resolve to undertake the agricultural tasks of the second cropping season. Every year, one must ensure the protection of cattle, protection of servants, protection of seeds, and protection of irrigation canals and watercourses. Likewise, protection of water reservoirs, tanks, and lakes, protection of implements such as spades and stakes, and protection of the threshing-floor must be maintained. Realizing that protecting fences and protecting fields is a primary duty, one should act accordingly with diligence. Conducted according to local traditions, agricultural work brings great prosperity, leading to supreme joy and the wealth and happiness of the three goals of life (dharma, artha, and kama). In suitable places, farming operations should be carried out for cultivating āḍhaka (pigeon pea), māṣa (black gram), caṇaka (chickpea), mudga (mung bean), kuluttha (horse gram), and tila (sesame). The sowing of seeds of marīci (black pepper) and jīraka (cumin) should also be done; from these, side-dishes (vyañjana) are said to be prepared. Various kinds of food are prepared in the world using grains and rice for the preservation of life, and the method for doing so constitutes the science of cookery (pāka-śāstra). A great treatise on cookery was composed by King Vīrasena, as well as by his son Nala and the great sage Garga. In those works, diverse methods for preparing rice and side-dishes are described; side-dishes impart palatability and flavor to cooked food in the world. Prepared everywhere using black gram, pigeon pea, pepper, salt, jaggery, and similar ingredients, food yields nourishment and good health to human beings. During the grain production season, clever farmers should cultivate both forest areas and village lands across the earth. At the proper season, for Āḍhaka (pigeon pea), Māṣa (black gram), Mudga (green gram), and other crops, in land sections ploughed with a plough and lightly moistened by rain water... Sowing of seeds is prescribed, whether using canal water or rain water, for Āḍhaka, Māṣa, Mudga, as well as Tila (sesame).

For Caṇaka (chickpea), both large and small varieties are specified in the treatises, to be sown in water-sprinkled land sectors and elevated spots here and there. The sowing of seeds such as Tila is commended by agricultural experts after four, five, or six days have elapsed. Sprouting of Āḍhaka and other crops then becomes visible in the ploughed field, which scriptures experts note depends on the richness of the soil. This is directly observed in various regions. On earth, a field for Vrīhi (rice) is designated as Jala-bhūmi (wetland). The land for fields of Māṣa and similar crops is known as Tāra-bhūmi (dry land). Therefore, agricultural work for Āḍhaka, Māṣa, and others by farmers... ...should be performed in Tāra fields, as declared by Bhārgava, following traditional custom or for convenience based on location. Sowing seeds of Māṣa and others in Vrīhi fields in certain places is also stated to be fruitful in this treatise of Kāśyapa. According to regional custom, or depending on place and time, whether in a section of Jala-bhūmi land or Tāra-bhūmi land... In a ploughed, mostly level field at the proper time, seeds of Bṛhad-āḍhaka (large pigeon pea) or Māṣa seeds... Mudga seeds, Caṇaka, Tila, Godhūma (wheat) seeds, Kuluttha (horse gram) seeds, Kīra seeds, and Kodrava... Seeds of Yavara, Marīci (pepper), Tūlerandaka, and seeds of Jīraka (cumin)... As well as seeds of Sarṣapa (mustard) and others, should be sown in season, row by row in orderly succession, in Tāra fields. Agriculture experts sow certain seeds, after moistening them with water, either in furrow rows or in various line-rows. Similarly, one should sow certain rows of good seeds that have not been soaked in water at the proper time, according to the custom and practice of one's own region. Observing the emergence of sprouts from seeds here and there on the two types of excellent land plots, the agricultural workers— Within one month, or slightly less or more in due course of time, abundant weeds indeed grow everywhere on the ground. Seeing them, farmers should cut, break, and completely uproot them along with their roots using hand-spades and other tools, removing them from that place. After removing weeds and the like, one should perform watering there on the ground where *āḍhakī* and other seeds have been sown. If there is excessive rainfall, destruction of seeds will surely occur; therefore, a light sprinkling with drops of water is best. Or the great sages state that this watering should be arranged using canal water for rows of *tila*, *godhūma*, *caṇaka*, *māṣa*, *mudga*, and *āḍhakī*. When weeds and other elements that cause destruction to seeds are removed, main and secondary branches grow from sprout to sprout. One should provide abundant nourishment at the root as for *kalama* rice; thus, when the host of weeds, tubers, and pests is destroyed, The growth of stalks and branches of *māṣa* and other crops is certainly assured, and beautiful blossoms and a charming appearance manifest.

After the flowering stage, a succession of ears of grain appears, and the production of tawny pods of *āḍhakī* and other crops is observed. In a period of three months, or in some places slightly more, the harvest of *māṣa*, *āḍhakī*, *caṇaka*, and *godhūma* is said to take place. At the root region on the soil, through the effect of watering, inner substance/essence develops in the pods; so it is taught. Thus, the manifestation of *māṣa*, *āḍhakī*, and *tila* on earth is ordained everywhere by divine will and revealed in the scriptures. As the inner substance thickens, rows of *māṣa* and other plants are seen everywhere bearing fruit in order at the tip of the ears. The falling of leaves, ripening, drooping, and the bending of the upper heads/tops are indicated by agricultural experts as signs of crop maturity. In accordance with the proper time, one should carry out irrigation for sesame as well as heaps of wheat growing on high/suitable lands. The emergence of ears of grain and the timing vary according to set factors, along with differences in species, appearance, and local farming practices. Suitable agricultural practices should be recognized according to the terrain; likewise, when the cluster of ears on pigeon-pea (āḍhakī) and other crops becomes dense, Harvesting is prescribed in the fully ripened field areas; during the harvest period, protection should be ensured by capable workers and guards. What is stated here yields great benefit for grain production; for the cut and harvested ears of grain placed at the threshing floor, Threshing with sticks and drying in sunlight are prescribed; the stalk-sticks of pigeon-pea and other crops serve as fodder for quadrupeds like bulls and horses.
