Farmers should protect these stalks intended for feeding by heaping them up at the threshing floor, at home, or in a suitable location. Storing the stalks and stems of pigeon-pea in cowpen courtyards or suitable places brings convenience and comfort. Straw and stalks of paddy, stems of pigeon-pea, as well as the leaves and stems of black gram (māṣa), wheat (godhūma), and chickpea (caṇaka), Which give life, complete nourishment, health, and comfort to quadrupeds and livestock across all seasons, The skilled farmer should gather, stack, and preserve, keeping them free from small impurities and damage. By using winnowing baskets, utilizing the wind, and thorough sifting or cleaning, the grains are made completely pure. Wheat, sesame, black gram, pigeon-pea, mustard, green gram (mudga), and other grains should be heaped up at the threshing floor. After drying them in the sun and thoroughly cleaning them, one should bring these chickpeas, pigeon-peas, and green grams into one's home. The farmer should store and protect prepared [crops and spices] separately in vessels at the proper time to secure prosperity and well-being. Experts in agriculture should skilfully cultivate grains, āḍhaka (pigeon pea), black pepper, and other produce on land according to regional customs. They should grow crops suited to the nature of each variety, appropriate for the specific land, season, and yields achievable through farming.

They should produce crops in villages, towns, and cities, as well as in adjacent lands and various divisions of fields. Undertaking agriculture according to rule is declared to bring great rewards, whether on moist soil or dry land suitable for farming. In every region and village, kodrava (kodo millet), yavara (sorghum/barley variant), and yava (barley) should be cultivated at the proper season, as these grains give nourishment. Their stalks sustain the life of cattle and other animals; therefore, kodrava and yavara are excellent in all regions. Having grown highly nutritious and essential crops, one should especially cultivate agastya (sesbania) and sugarcane stalks suitable for the soil. Sugarcane farming is highly praised as immensely fruitful; it is a chief food for elephants and the source of sugar and jaggery. Strong sugarcane stalks grow well over time in marshy lands, or in dry land areas, especially in suitable fields. Making long rows of pits, one should plant [the stalks] there; this method applies to kadalī (banana/plantain) and puṇḍra sugarcane across the earth. Seed-sowing is not observed for these, either directly or in texts; planting is done in autumn or at another time prescribed by the region. Farmers should place sugarcane stalks into pits; placing them, watering, and filling the pits with soil are to be done in due order. After ten days have passed, sprouts emerge from their base; from these sugarcane sprouts, leaves and stalks then grow forth. Within two or three months, depending on the site, full foliage growth is assuredly achieved, yielding fruitful results. Knowing the height of the row of sugarcane stalks to reach the height of a man or even taller, the expert in agriculture— —should diligently arrange for daily watering in the pit around their base, and protect them especially at the appropriate time. Utmost protection of these sugarcanes from wind and weather should be provided. In this manner, the method for plantain (*kadalī*) trees on earth has also been described. Plantain constantly yields fruit, and its varieties are considered diverse according to regional practices and seasonal conditions, O experts in agriculture. One should cultivate plantain and sugarcane stalks in all seasons; these are said to be constantly fruit-yielding in every region. Whether on a mountain ridge or on a peak, or in hard soil, the wise cultivator, knowing the fertility of the soil— —should grow plantain and sugarcane stalk for easy success; these are declared to be constantly fruit-yielding in all lands. The knower of soil should not cultivate them in alkaline or severely defective land; therefore, in a plot endowed with good features, the wise person— —should grow pulse crops such as chickpea (*caṇaka*), pigeon pea (*āḍhakī*), and green gram (*mudga*), protect them, and bring the harvested produce home. To obtain cotton cloth, one should cultivate cotton trees (*picu-vṛkṣa* / *tūla-vṛkṣa*) and their rows in high land or appropriate places. Likewise, in warm regions, the farmer should cultivate that which yields prosperity as handed down through traditional instruction.

Or based on direct observation, the skillful farmer should grow all these crops near the threshing-floor area, at the edge of the village, or along the village boundary. Or inside pleasure gardens, in suitable plots, near the banks of water reservoirs, or on elevated village homestead land. Thus the growth of cotton plants and the orderly prosperity of other crops is declared as commendable by eminent sages well-versed in the scriptures. Thus ends the first section titled "Description of the Order of Cultivation of Grains and Other Crops" in the *Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkta*. Those who are knowledgeable in agricultural operations everywhere in the world, along with virtuous Brāhmaṇas, should always abide by the king's command. In the paddy field, one should sequentially cultivate śāli rice and other crops at the proper time; similarly, on high dry lands (tāra-kṣetra), one should grow chickpeas (caṇaka) and other crops. By this, the complete means of sustenance is provided, through varieties of śāli rice as well as supplementary ingredients. Complete satisfaction is not seen on earth merely through pulses like āḍhaka; therefore, one should cultivate delicious vegetables and other plants there. One should grow jaṭikā, rāśi-jaṭikā, creepers (vallikā), wild creepers (vana-vallikā), pointed gourds (paṭolikā), eggplants (vārtāka), and ṣavakā as well. Likewise, various vegetables, pumpkins (kūṣmāṇḍa), kalāṭaka, coriander (kustumburu), kalāṭa, elephant-foot yam (sūraṇa), and śākuṭa should be grown. Farmers should cultivate turmeric (haridrā), ginger (śuṇṭhī), wild varieties growing on dry land, and various juicy plants originating on high ground. They should cultivate them in agricultural order to fulfill dietary requirements; in my opinion, these are the primary vegetable substances. In some remaining instances, vegetables and other plants are described as distinct according to differences in species, appearance, taste, and color. Farmers should cultivate onion (palāṇḍu), and the growing of grapes (drākṣā), spikenard (nalada), cardamom (elā), and other crops should also be carried out on various elevated grounds. Whether on high dry land or on wet land, cultivation should be appropriate for the season, suited to the region, and based on traditional sequence. Understanding the proper procedure, the wise person should cultivate vegetable plants, taking grain crops as primary and pulse crops as secondary. Vegetables (*śāka-dravya*) form the third category produced through the sequence of agricultural practices, while ghee, milk, and curd form the fourth category described. These four types of substances constitute the system of food (*bhojya-kalpa*); it enhances the delight of all the gods in this world. It is the foundation for the stability of life for all human beings, bestowing nourishment and health, as well as increasing intellect and lifespan. Created by *Brahmā* at the time of creation across all lands, it is through this system of food that the earth remains endued with life. From that time onwards, *Brahmā*'s creation achieved fulfillment across all countries and in diverse fields on earth. For great sages, ascetics, and all human beings everywhere, this system of food is declared to bestow the fruits of the three goals of life (*trivarga*).

Therefore, the cultivation of vegetables and other food crops should be specially undertaken by farmers in villages and in towns. Likewise in forests and forest glades possessing good characteristics, near human habitations, and especially close to water reservoirs. The work of cultivating vegetables and other crops is certainly fruitful, whether carried out in spring, summer, or winter in suitable locations. For crops such as eggplants (*vārtāka*), creepers, garlic/spices (*jaṭika*), pepper (*marīcī*), and others, those desiring sprouts should prepare the surface of a plowed field. Seeds of eggplant and other plants, after being dried in the sun, should be sown in ground enriched with cow dung and organic manure. Experts should lay out the seeds for germination, water them, and then cover the seedbed with straw in due order. When three days have elapsed at the seedbed site in this manner, the emergence of sprouts takes place according to rule. After twenty days, when a sturdy network of saplings has formed, the wise farmer should dig them up and transplant them into a properly plowed field. Watering the roots immediately at that time preserves life; one should grow eggplants and other plants in raised circular basins (*ālavāla*). One should cultivate paṭolikā (pointed gourd) and creeping vines on a trellis structure (kāyamāna) to facilitate the proper growth of the creepers. A wise person should undertake the cultivation of vegetable crops in irrigated fields during the summer season without waiting for the rainy season, as well as at other times, which yields good results. One should plant the tubers of edible plants, tubers of sūraṇa (elephant-foot yam), and turmeric roots in basins (ālavāla) or suitable spots. Cultivating them on dry land or in warm soil yields successful agricultural fruits; thus, the cultivation of various types of creeper plants is considered manifold. One should grow kūṣmāṇḍa (pumpkin), vana-kūṣmāṇḍa (wild pumpkin), cardamoms (elā), nalada (spikenard), and other principal herbs on elevated land, and nāgavallī (betel vine) in suitable locations. A wise farmer should cultivate plantains (kadalī), sugarcane (ikṣudaṇḍa), betel vine (nāgavallī), and betel-nut trees (pūgī) in wetland fields, gardens, and pleasure-groves. One should also grow rambhā and mocā (varieties of banana/plantain), fruit-bearing panasa (jackfruit), likuca (monkey-jack), rasāla (sweet mango), āmra (mango), and jambū (rose-apple). An expert in agriculture should also nurture coconut trees (nārikela) in the backyard of houses, in orchards, or in other available spaces. Whether on high grounds or in marshy lands, according to the availability of land in the region, Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, As well as Vaiśyas, Śūdras, people of mixed castes, hunters, and warriors alike, should practice agriculture on their own lands to the best of their ability. One should cultivate coriander (dhānyāka), sūraṇa, creepers, kūṣmāṇḍa, paṭolikā, and other plants like jaṭilā prescribed in the treatises, in due order. First, plowing the land, and second, applying cow-dung manure to enrich the soil—this is known to be the proper method for enhancing soil fertility.

In that field, multi-mouthed basins (ālavāla) should be prepared, and in these active basins, one should plant eggplant (vārtāka) and other vegetables. Even in plots meant for jasmine (mālatī, kunda), cāmpeya, kuṭaja, and other flowering plants, multi-mouthed basins suited to the location should be constructed. Sowing seeds or planting sprouts around the edges of the basin should be carried out according to local customs and proper seasonal timing. Then, after the passage of one month, the removal of the host of enemy weeds and grass from the base of vārtāka (eggplant) and other plants is prescribed. Every five days or six days, a wise person should tend to the base of vārtāka and other plants through the water basin (ālavāla) around the roots. One should perform irrigation, especially during the summer season; frequent watering eliminates dry weeds and keeps the root-basin clear. This is declared by sages expert in the scriptures to yield great fruit. Sometimes, on the leaf-clusters of vegetables, vārtākas, and similar plants, As well as on the creepers of paṭolikā (pointed gourd), ṣavakās, kūṣmāṇḍa (pumpkins/gourds), kalāṭas, and sūraṇa (yam), And on śākuṭas, turmeric (haridrā), and ginger (ārdraka), damage caused by pests and insects devouring the foliage is observed. Therefore, to eliminate the harm caused by insects and pests, farmers should dust them with ash-powder or sprinkle water mixed with lime/chalk. One should perform these tasks systematically at the right time according to local custom, regarding the sowing of seeds as well as the removal of weeds and grass. In nurturing creepers and plants during the flowering season, whatever procedure is established in the world and executed by agricultural experts, One should personally observe and apply all of that based on traditional teaching, for paṭolikās, vārtākas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and other plants on the earth. Wise farmers should likewise apply appropriate cultivation techniques to jambīra (lime), likuca (breadfruit/citron), elā (cardamom), drākṣā (grapes), kharjūra (date palm), and the like. They should organize agricultural work according to regional tradition, proper sequence, and seasonal fitness, for the purpose of securing nutritious, edible, and tasty food. Among those crops, some are praised as delicious in the form of leaves; others are useful as flowers, while others yield value in the form of fruits. Others are useful in the form of bark/shoots, and still others in the form of bulbs/roots, sequentially at the onset of flowering, during flowering, and after flowering. Some parts are edible and some are drinkable, especially in the case of the kadalī (banana plant); the root-bulb, stem, flower, and tender sheath of kadalī are all utilized. Fruits or roots that are always sweet and agreeable to the palate are prescribed as fit for consumption by the truth-seeing sages. The tender harvest of paṭolikā (snake gourd), vārtākā (eggplant), and leafy vegetables possesses a sweeter juice during their tender young stage. Therefore, harvesting them while tender is praised.

However, in the case of panasa (jackfruit), rasāla (mango), and kūṣmāṇḍa (gourd)... ...harvesting at middle age yields a sweeter juice; likewise for ikṣu (sugarcane), nārikela (coconut), and likuca (breadfruit/monkey jack). For mangoes and similar fruits, when harvested in their fully mature final stage, the juice is described as ideal for culinary preparations (temana) and processing. Thus, following local traditions and family customs, as well as the rules stated in culinary science regarding time and combination of ingredients... ...and considering the balance of bodily humors like pitta in one's own body, agricultural experts in the world should undertake the cultivation of paṭola and other crops. They should protect and nurture these crops at home, in fields, pleasure gardens, private lands, wet paddy fields (kedāra), or along the banks of step-wells and lakes. Especially below or near the mouth of water reservoirs, one should plant kadalī (banana), pūga (areca nut), punnāga, nārikela (coconut), and āmra (mango) trees. One should skillfully cultivate panasa (jackfruit), elā (cardamom), drākṣā (grapes), mālatī jasmine, as well as eggplants, creepers, and gourds. Various leafy vegetables, drinkables, eatables, and chewables should be preserved and carefully raised according to the proper seasonal cycles of farming. In every region, whether during spring (vasanta), summer (grīṣma), the rainy season (varṣā), autumn (śarat), or early winter (hemanta)... ...and even during late winter (śiśira), one should construct water-basins (ālavāla) in various fields appropriate to each respective season. Vegetables, leaves, bark, flowers, tubers, or rich juices that promote health and strength should be produced on earth through systematic agriculture. Agricultural experts should foster these and gather excellent yield, such as elā (cardamom), lavaṅga (cloves), ārddraka (ginger), pūga (areca nut), and tāmbūla (betel) vines. Sugarcane stalks, plantain trees, and various other creepers should be cultivated along the borders of fields or on elevated land plots. Other beneficial plants such as long pepper (pippalī) and various life-enhancing medicinal creepers... ...should be grown particularly according to the suitability of each field, at the proper season, and following traditional custom as instructed by ancient sages. Whatever has been declared in the scriptures by ancient sages as achievable through agriculture and bringing happiness to all living beings... ...farmers as well as Brāhmaṇas should diligently cultivate with proper skill in their respective fields for the protection and sustenance of their families. For the gratification of the gods, agriculture is declared to be practiced on earth by Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others as well. This knowledge was recorded in treatises by sages who perceived the truth. At the beginning of the eon (kalpa), Brahmā, the creator... ...created various seeds and placed them upon the earth specifically to fulfill the prayer of the earth goddess (Bhūmidevī) for the creation of beings. "A single seed shall take manifold forms and yield abundant fruit for human beings—there is no doubt about this." Thus was heard what was spoken of old by Bhūmi, the consort of Viṣṇu. That science of agriculture taught by Bhūmi was brought to the earth by the sages.

It was preserved by kings bearing the duty of protecting the world, and in course of time it was studied especially by the Śūdras. From then onward, the treatise named Kṛṣi was extensively expanded and preserved by the inhabitants of the earth in accordance with the rainy seasons. Thus over a long period of time, human beings in various lands studied each part of the science of agriculture with devotion. Agriculture was carried out in their own fields and paddy-plots, full yields were obtained, and all living creatures were nourished. Especially their own subjects, with the assistance of divine kings; therefore, in all regions, kings should assist in agricultural activities. The sages of old declared that supreme assistance should be given; for without the help of kings on this agricultural earth... ...in a country, town, or village, agriculture does not yield its full fruits—this has been observed directly by subjects and servants alike. Therefore, kings everywhere must render agricultural assistance, which yields great benefits, for the well-being and prosperity of regions and nations. For the increase of their own well-being, for supreme fame, to please the gods, and to establish firmly their own dharma. Giving land and cows to learned *brāhmaṇa*s and *śrotriya*s of various *gotra*s, as well as the digging of canals (*kulyā*)... ...for the benefit of *brāhmaṇa*s, *vaiśya*s, *śūdra*s, and others who are incapable of manual agricultural work, in manifold ways... ...assistance in agriculture should be rendered in according with royal duty (*rājadharma*), such as digging step-wells (*vāpī*), wells (*kūpa*), ponds (*taḍāga*), and reservoirs (*hrada*)... ...and setting up water-wheels (*ghaṭīyantra*) for water reservoirs, as well as suppressing in various ways thieves who destroy crops... ...and punishing them for the fame of virtuous beings and the attainment of *dharma*. Thus, manifold assistance in agricultural work is firmly prescribed. All this, as declared by the sage, must be performed by rulers of the earth in every village, city, country, or any place whatsoever. For the protection of subjects incapable of agricultural labor, and in populated cities, capitals, and residential areas... ...or for their benefit, kings should designate fertile fields of various types, or circles of fields of two kinds on earth. Undertaking agricultural work at the proper time and in due order, kings should employ their servants and especially their subjects. Employing people of mixed origin, destitute individuals, and *śūdra*s in farming sites, they should cultivate various grains and crops there. Likewise, crops such as āḍhaka (pigeon pea), vegetables, and flowers primarily including jasmine (mallī) and champaka should be cultivated appropriately in suitable places. They should immensely increase the heaps of vegetable commodities as well as heaps of grains to foster the welfare and prosperity of their subjects. Heaps of āḍhakī, caṇaka (chickpea), sesame, māṣa (black gram), and sarṣapa (mustard), as well as clusters of grapes and other fruits, And heaps of various seasonal fruits—the king, having arranged them, should display/store them for the happiness and comfort of the people.

Either in marketplace shops or in locations specially constructed for that purpose, in public squares, courtyards, or open uncovered places, Or in market stalls and shed-structures; all the goods mentioned earlier and whatever else brings comfort, Blankets, various garments, curd, milk, etc., and diverse food articles—chewable and eatable—available on earth, Beneficial jaggery and oil obtained through agricultural produce, and whatever other commodity is mentioned here—all that, the king, In villages, towns, cities, and especially in the capital city, should bring to market areas for commercial transactions. Settling especially the Vaiśyas skilled in commerce, the king should employ wealthy merchants for buying and selling. Whatever is obtained through agricultural operations in months such as spring, whatever is derived through mechanical devices, and whatever is obtained from weavers, Whatever is obtained from oil-pressers and whatever is obtained from garland-makers like perfumes and aromatic goods on earth—all that the ruler of the earth, Having procured all of that for securing the happiness of his subjects, in villages, towns, cities, and especially in the capital, In shops, halls, courtyards, and various places, the king should establish and protect the Vaiśyas appointed there. The king should institute standard measures such as prastha, kubja, droṇa, nāḍikā, and smaller ones for measuring grains, āḍhaka, and other commodities. The king should have measuring vessels like *prastha* made with iron plates and heartwood boards, and implement them everywhere throughout the land. Likewise, for weighing oil and other substances, he should fix a *pala* measure constructed with iron pieces to maintain a uniform standard everywhere. He should institute uniform shapes and uniform prices in that country, and make those standard measures known among the *vaiśya*s and rural inhabitants. He should communicate these through his servants and especially through *brāhmaṇa*s, making the balance beam specifically of bronze or brass. For weighing vegetables and other produce, the king, together with his chief ministers, should systematically institute measures like *pala* and *prastha* everywhere. Having specially stamped the measures, the king should implement them everywhere in the country to regulate the knowledge of transactions and prices of grains and other goods. He should proclaim this rule everywhere in every region, in every village and every house, systematically for the happiness of his subjects. Regarding the heaps of grain commodities, oil, cloth, vegetables, and other agricultural produce, Whatever diverse assistance has been prescribed in the śāstras by ancient sages, the king should provide all of it for the attainment of general welfare. Scholars learned in the śāstras affirm that without agriculture, there can be no happiness or sustenance on earth for two-legged or four-legged beings. Therefore, for pleasing the deities and protecting the subjects, devotion and dedication to agricultural work depend entirely upon the king. Guided especially by royal priests, *brāhmaṇa*s, and ministers, the ruler or *kṣatriya* who bears the burden of protecting the people, Agriculture is praised as the highest among all endeavors; he should protect and foster it in his lands with effort and systematic method.

Thus, the king should systematically lay out a pleasure garden or grove in the village, town, or especially in the capital city, An orchard of trees outside or in the center of the city, specially intended for the recreation and enjoyment of the ladies of the inner court. The wise ruler should establish pleasure-gardens and orchards at the edge of the forest, also for growing valuable trees such as sandalwood. He should provide assistance for constructing houses for his subjects, and plant delightful trees laden with fruit in the garden areas around the palace. The king should systematically grow various trees such as plantain, banana, lemon, citron, and long pepper. He should also cultivate other medicinal creepers, nalada (spikenard), various types of kuśa and kāśa grasses, tulası̄, and bilva trees. The king should everywhere cultivate numerous flowers suitable for worship that are fragrant and available in season. He should judiciously grow other plants that promote family health, and lay out temple gardens in sacred locations for festivals. The king should establish these gardens either within or outside the village, according to available space and local traditions. Likewise, on the palace grounds, he should establish an excellent garden for women, rich with charming groves of trees and adorned with mālatī and other flowers. Similarly, the king should establish such a garden outside the capital city to increase the delight of his subjects. Thus, in a forest, at the forest fringe, or on mountain slopes, he should establish a great forest resplendent with diverse trees. The king should order the preservation of seeds of various tree species there, along with fruits, flowers, wooden planks, and timber blocks. By this, assistance for house construction for the subjects is ensured; therefore, the king who bears the duty of protecting the land... ...should, in vast expanses of land or along boundary walls, plant karañja, naktamāla, eraṇḍa (castor), and bhūrja (birch). He should also plant arjuna, sarja, nīpa, kadamba, śigru, śamī, maruvaka, and devadāru trees. And in appropriate places, śrīparṇikā, tinduka, vaṭa (banyan), plakṣa, bhadradāru, and priyaṅgu. The ruler should plant Vibhītaka, Āmalakī, Haimavatī, Karṇikāra, Likuča, and Nimba trees in appropriate places. The king should also plant Aśoka, Śirīṣa, Dāḍima, Jambū, Kapittha, and Bhadraka trees all around. Likewise, Cāmpeyaka, Kurabaka, various varieties of Karṇika, Tāpiñcha, Tamāla, and Sinduvāra trees should be grown. He should especially plant large trees such as Tintriṇī (tamarind), bamboo in places, as well as Cūta, Rasāla, Āmra (mango varieties), and Badarī trees. So also wild forest trees, Madhūka, Pīlu, Punnāga, Paribhadra, and Kovidāra trees should be planted. Thus, the ruler of the earth should systematically plant valuable trees of various species and forms, and protect them by watering. Thus, the great forest or those along riverbanks should be duly protected from forest fire, wild ferocious animals, and thieves.

In regions such as Gāndhāra, Kunti, Pañcāla, Kāśmīra, Avanti, Sindhu, Nepāla, Niṣadha, Kosala, and Aṅga; And in places like Dhūrjara, Avanti, Saurāṣṭra, and in various regions on fertile land, the king— Should establish a great forest shining in all directions with groves of all kinds of trees, equipped all around with ponds, canals, and stepped wells. Having had it planted systematically by farmers and his subjects, he should protect it through heroes, soldiers, and warriors for the attainment of prosperity and happiness. Near a mountain or inside a forest, the ruler of the earth should examine and safeguard mines that yield various metals. Examining the subterranean mineral veins, he should protect them wherever found—mines of iron ore, brass, gold, as well as silver, As well as red ochre (gairika), procuring them with effort for the welfare of the realm; and with blacksmiths skilled in ironwork and carpenters, And with goldsmiths, in villages as well as cities, he should systematically arrange for the manufacture of various weapons. Having distributed suitable agricultural implements to the rural populace, and for the protection of the city, palace, fort, and other places, the king— —should also place and maintain various types of weapons among the soldiers in appropriate locations and army encampments. With gold, silver, minerals, corals harvested from ocean waves, and pearls in proper order, the king— —having fashioned a variety of ornaments, should especially offer them first to the deities, and then to the Brāhmaṇas. Wearing them himself and suitably adorning the queen as well as the palace women with those respective ornaments— —filled with supreme joy, he should protect this earth. Thus the king should bring happiness to all in every region. The ruler should acquire various kinds of wealth from all sides, according to different methods or over the course of time. Understanding the variations in agricultural practices, the methods of sowing seeds, and the division of farming activities according to cold and hot regions— —as well as considering cattle grazing, rainfall patterns, and the condition of water reservoirs, knowing the manifold yields— —one should engage in agricultural operations according to the fertility of the field. When the king is pleased, everything succeeds on earth. If the king is displeased, everything is surely destroyed. Therefore, for the prosperity and abundance of the nation, the ruler of the earth should remain pleased. Collecting tax revenue, coins, or grain from the farmers in due order, the king should protect the entire earth with all its moving and non-moving beings— —like his own family, through righteous means. Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and all other people, having received support for agricultural activities directly from the king, with devotion— —and carrying out agriculture on the land according to proper time and custom, while paying their tax revenue, contribute to the growth and welfare of the nation. Having nourished the gods, guests, and one's own family in due order, particularly in accordance with the path of Dharma as prescribed.

Likewise, those whose fame adorns all quarters should protect them to the best of their ability, especially in a village, a district, or a city. Cherishing mutual affection, receiving the support of the king, and engaged in the duties of their respective castes and life-stages, may they flourish greatly upon the earth! Prompted by the king's order, the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and others as well, should engage in agriculture at the proper time, especially in fertile soil. Having carried out various kinds of agriculture according to the specified method, they should make heaps of various grains, measured by the āḍhaka measure. They should bring the heaps of black pepper, mustard seeds, and other produce to their homes, having dried them in the sun at the proper time and in due order. They should prepare them daily for cooking to satisfy the gods; indeed, the work of cooking should be performed by virtuous women according to divine ordinance. Thus the honouring of the gods and guests will become fruitful, and thereafter the protection of the subjects is surely assured by the lord of sages. Therefore, a Brahmana knowing the Dharma, after understanding the classification of edible and inedible substances of various kinds, should engage a chaste woman in cooking. Food prepared from pilu fruit and kodrava grain is unfit for gods and Brahmanas, as are pure white eggplant (sveta-vartaka), garlic, and grinjana (carrots/onions). Onions, mushrooms, plant exudate (resins), and produce grown in unholy or bad places are likewise unfit for consumption by Brahmanas. A Brahmana should avoid large pumpkins, panna [?], shigru (moringa), piluka, as well as crops grown in improper places. A twice-born (dvija) should carefully avoid main food items that have been contaminated at home by ants, flies, or worms. Likewise, food defiled by dogs, roosters, etc., food given without trust, or food touched and defiled by fingernails should be avoided. A dvija should avoid food contaminated with chaff, threads, etc., as well as food defiled or smelled by cats inside the house. Food items defiled by musk-rats, mice, etc., should all be avoided with care, especially by a Brahmana. Anyone on earth seeking his own well-being should never eat food defiled, smelled, or touched by low or impure individuals. All food served in an impure place, left over from a bite, or fallen on the ground should be completely discarded. Sages declare food to be inedible—for the sake of attaining fame and prosperity—if it has not been offered first to guests and especially to the deities. Food served at improper times, during eclipses, cooked in an unsuited place, or unwashed with water is also unfit to eat. Whether it be grain, a heap of vegetables, delicacies, or chewable food, if contaminated, it is declared inedible, especially for Brahmanas. Food cooked by an unrefined person, defiled by excrement or urine, contaminated with hair, or eaten from first by oneself (before offering) is unfit.

One should avoid food cooked by an unbathed person, food served directly by bare hand, or food served with the left hand. The best of the twice-born (dvija) should avoid food served with a piece of iron or from wooden vessels and baskets, as well as stale food (paryuṣita). Food cooked in another's house and brought to one's own home is declared unfit for eating by sages well-versed in the scriptures. A dvija should not eat curd-rice or sesame-rice at night, nor eat in moonlight without a lamp. Likewise, eating directly on bare ground or eating in the dark is specified as blameworthy by foremost sages and gods alike. Similarly, foamy water, the first rainwater/floodwater of rivers, rain falling directly from the sky, and torrential stream water should be avoided. A wise person should carefully avoid water touched by untouchables, milk of camels, milk of single-hoofed animals, and milk of two-hoofed animals (forbidden types). Likewise, salted milk, human milk, cow's milk from which the calf has been removed, or milk drawn while another calf is present are forbidden. Cow's milk or goat's milk that has become impure, as well as milk kept in a copper vessel, are known by the wise to be censurable and fit to be discarded. Therefore, a learned Vipra (Brahmana) knowing dharma should understand the rules of edible and inedible foods and prepare meals according to prescribed tradition to attain spiritual perfection. This strict rule is not prescribed for Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras on earth by the truth-perceiving sages. Meat-eating is definitively not a sin for them; Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others on earth— —having understood the order of fit and unfit foods according to regional customs, should consume food only after offering it first to the deity. Thus cleansed of sins, they shine radiant with faith and devotion; therefore, in all regions, Brāhmaṇas as well as Kṣatriyas— —and Vaiśyas should always utilize pure materials such as rice grains, as well as fresh and purifying vegetable items. Water, milk, curd, clarified butter (ghṛta), fresh butter (navanīta), oil, leafy greens, and utensils [should be used] in due order. Either by oneself or together with one's virtuous wives in their respective homes, on a plot of ground smeared with cow dung, preparing a hearth that is clean, white, and provided with fuel, After worshiping specifically the Earth and Vasava (Indra), as well as Yama, Agni, Varuna, and especially Brahma, Having cooked food at the proper time in pots, jars, and other vessels, it should then be set down in a clean place, resplendent with the six tastes and other qualities.

Various foods to be chewed (bhakṣya) and eaten (bhojya), such as vaṭaka cakes and the like, cooked with oil, ghee, and other ingredients following the rules of culinary science (pākaśāstra), Accompanied by sugar, jaggery, diverse side dishes, and various seasoned gravies along with special spices, Having prepared the food with faith and devotion at the proper time and in due order, one should place it at the altar of divine worship or within the house. They should fill baskets and vessels as appropriate for offering to the gods; all this is enjoined by the scriptures. Thus ends the third part titled "Description of the Order of Edible and Inedible Foodstuffs" in the Kāśyapīya Kṛṣisūkti. Cooking activity is of two kinds: daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*). Daily cooking is always fit to receive the grace and auspicious glance of the Lord of Gods. Occasional cooking is similar, though there is a distinction of eligible recipients/vessels there. The collection of food fit for the gods is called *havya*. This very food is ordained by the scriptures for guests and subjects as fit to be eaten (*bhojya*), whereas food offered to the ancestors (*pitṛs*) is designated as *kavya*. That (*kavya*) food should be consumed along with one's own kinsmen, as declared by scholars of scripture. Diverse forms of the Lord of Gods are declared worthy of worship. Knowing the various forms such as the *Śivalinga*, the *Sālagrāma* stone, and the various metallic incarnations/manifestations of Viṣṇu, an excellent twice-born (*dvijottama*)... ...or a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya, performing his evening twilight rituals (*saṁdhyā-karma*) according to rule and capacity, should arrange for the worship of the deity. All of that is prescribed in scriptures to be done with royal honors (*rājopacāra*), beginning with mouth-rinsing (*gaṇḍūṣa*), sipping water (*ācamana*), bathing, and wearing fresh clothes. Having arranged a seat for dining, filled with faith and devotion, he should offer the excellent variety of food, rice, and dishes cooked by virtuous women... ...for the satisfaction of the deity, adorned with various side dishes: jaggery-rice (*guḍānna*), milk-pudding rice (*pāyasānna*), and similarly sesame-rice (*tilānna*). As well as curd-rice (*dadhyanna*), mung-bean rice (*mudgānna*), sweet pancakes (*apūpa*), vada (*vaṭaka*), wheat-vada, and flatbreads (*polikā*) fit for royalty. Sweet dumplings (*modaka*), sugar boondi (*śarkarā-bandi*), combined with raisins, cardamom, saffron ingredients, and rich crystalline sugar. Or *payogalakabandī* (a milk preparation) or varied dishes, prepared properly according to the cooking procedure, sweet and suitable for the season. Dishes mixed with *māṣa* (black gram) and *taṇḍula* (rice), seasoned with salt and other flavors, such as *ḍala* and *mahāḍala*, properly cooked and mixed with ghee. The same cooked *ḍala* of various shapes, tasting like nectar, combined with curd, or accompanied by ghee and sugar. Or one should prepare sugary *jalepikā* (*jalebi*), combined with *mudga* (green gram) and *godhūma* (wheat), along with ghee and rich in *māṣa* (black gram). Sweet, salty, as well as pungent, bitter, sour, and sometimes astringent—thus the food substances possessing the six tastes (*ṣaḍrasa*) are described.

Using the flours of *godhūma* (wheat), *māṣa* (black gram), *mudga* (green gram), and *caṇaka* (chickpea), various eatables such as *ḍala*, as well as chewable foods and beverages, are prepared.
Chewable foods cooked in due course that delight the tongue, properly fried in oil or in ghee at the appropriate time.
Staple grains, curries and soups (*temana*), dishes rich in flavor, and various cooked eatables should be offered with faith and devotion.
All these varieties of eatables and foods should be cooked systematically in the kitchen using pure ingredients according to prescribed rules.
O best of brahmins, after offering these with devotion following the ritual order of divine worship to Lord Viṣṇu of infinite radiance, who is seated at the altar of worship/dining.
Having completed the ceremonial service, offering flowers, fragrant unguents, fanning with *cāmara* (chauri) and fans, as well as chanting hymns of praise.
All divine worship is declared to be conducted with royal honors (*rājopacāra*), arranged specially during daily (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites.
Daily satisfying at the proper time the Lord of the Universe, who bestows cherished desires, through devotional prayers, prostrations, and worship.
Food cooked daily with reverence using pure agricultural produce is offered first to Vāsudeva, Kṛṣṇa, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Soul, and then systematically served to guests and one's own family.
Food suitable for eating and various other eatables cooked in the kitchen, endowed with the six tastes, should be served for the purpose of self-sustenance.
The foremost among the twice-born (brāhmaṇas) should serve the food in dining vessels, especially on plantain (banana) leaves, and feed the guests with great affection.
Having offered them betel leaves along with lime in due order, the brāhmaṇas who are best among the knowers of dharma perform these duties in the world by the king's command.
One should devoutly observe both the sacrifice to the gods (deva-yajña) and the sacrifice to all living beings (bhūta-yajña) on this earth, which are righteous, fame-bestowing, and life-prolonging.
For the attainment of the welfare of the family, the king, and especially the nation, this eternal duty must indeed be performed—so declared the sage Kāśyapa for the benefit of all the world.
